options: A list of every index and its fragmentation percentage
SQL Server's internal perfmon-style counters, queryable directly with T-SQL
The full text of every stored procedure on the instance
Only the login history for the last 30 days
questions.explain: sys.dm_os_performance_counters exposes the same counters Performance Monitor (perfmon) graphs, as queryable rows.

questions.q: What does a sustained drop in Page life expectancy, relative to this server's own baseline, generally signal?
options: That tempdb has run out of disk space
That the recovery model was changed to SIMPLE
A successful index rebuild
Memory pressure — data pages are being pushed out of the buffer pool faster than normal
questions.explain: Page life expectancy estimates how long a page stays in memory; a sustained drop versus baseline is a classic memory pressure signal.

options: Read/write I/O stats, including stall time, for every database file on the instance
Only the files belonging to tempdb
The list of logins with file-level permissions
The fragmentation level of every index
questions.explain: Passing NULL, NULL for database_id and file_id returns I/O stats for every file across every database on the instance.

questions.q: What does a high average value of io_stall_read_ms / num_of_reads for a data file generally indicate?
options: The query optimizer chose a bad execution plan
Statistics on that file's table are out of date
The database is in the wrong recovery model
The storage subsystem is slow to respond to reads on that file, not necessarily a problem with the query itself
questions.explain: A high average read stall points at storage responsiveness, distinct from query design or plan choice issues.

questions.q: Why does the guide emphasize reading page life expectancy and I/O stalls together, rather than in isolation?
options: Because SQL Server only reports one counter at a time
Because a dropping page life expectancy combined with high I/O stalls on the same file suggests a compounding problem — memory pressure forcing rereads from slow storage
Because only one of the two counters is ever accurate
Because they measure the exact same thing and are redundant
questions.explain: The two signals reinforce each other: memory pressure evicts pages, which then have to be reread from storage that is itself slow, compounding the problem.
